session.question: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?
session.answer:
Coronary artery calcifications on routine trauma CT were associated with a higher risk of in-hospital complications. Left main coronary artery calcification was independently associated with developing any complication, with an odds ratio of 3.9 (95% CI 1.7–8.9). An increasing number of calcified coronary arteries showed a graded trend toward more complications, indicating a burden–response relationship. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

The complications described included general clinical complications such as pneumonia and delirium. In addition, more extensive coronary calcification was significantly associated with an adverse discharge condition on the Glasgow Outcome Scale, suggesting worse short-term functional outcome at discharge. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

Overall, the available evidence indicates that coronary artery calcification is a marker of elevated peri-trauma risk, identifying patients more likely to develop clinical complications and to have poorer discharge outcomes. Pulmonary emphysema and aortic calcifications were not associated with complications in this cohort. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

pqac-980529f7: This study evaluated whether coronary artery calcification score (CACS) and MESA percentiles predict mortality in 4,985 symptomatic patients. Coronary calcification was associated with adverse outcomes in that higher absolute CACS predicted all-cause mortality with moderately good performance. Over a median 4.4 years, 116 patients died (53 women, 63 men). The authors concluded that absolute CACS is useful for mortality risk prediction, while MESA percentiles did not improve prediction. They also noted that adding degree of stenosis may slightly improve mortality risk prediction in women, suggesting calcification relates to clinically important complications and death in symptomatic individuals.
From Klaske R Siegersma, Floor Groepenhoff, Anouk L M Eikendal, Willemijn J op den Brouw, Tim Leiner, Yolande Appelman, Igor I Tulevski, G Aernout Somsen, N Charlotte Onland-Moret, Leonard Hofstra, and Hester M den Ruijter. Coronary calcification measures predict mortality in symptomatic women and men. Open Heart, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1136/openhrt-2022-002005, doi:10.1136/openhrt-2022-002005.

pqac-2fdd7379: The excerpt is about lower-limb arterial calcification in hemodialysis patients, not coronary artery calcification. It reports that higher calcification scores in the superficial femoral and below-knee arteries were linked to worse long-term clinical outcomes, especially cardiovascular events, mortality, and limb amputations. In multivariate analysis, superficial femoral artery calcification was an independent predictor of 10-year cardiovascular events and amputations. Kaplan–Meier analysis also showed higher calcification associated with cardiovascular events and mortality. No direct information is given here about coronary artery calcifications or their complications.
From Takayasu Ohtake, Ayaka Mitomo, Mizuki Yamano, Toshihiro Shimizu, Yasuhiro Mochida, Kunihiro Ishioka, Machiko Oka, Kyoko Maesato, Hidekazu Moriya, Sumi Hidaka, Milanga Mwanatambwe, and Shuzo Kobayashi. Impact of arterial calcification of the lower limbs on long-term clinical outcomes in patients on hemodialysis. Journal of Clinical Medicine, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm12041299, doi:10.3390/jcm12041299.

pqac-efff1ffb: The excerpt describes a case report of pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) in a 60-year-old woman who underwent detailed coronary artery disease evaluation. Intravascular imaging suggested fragmented and calcified elastic fibers in the internal elastic lamina, implying a possible mechanism for coronary artery disease in PXE. However, the excerpt does not discuss how coronary artery calcifications are associated with specific complications, nor does it provide procedural or general clinical complication data.
From Tomohiro Fujisaki, Masanobu Ishii, Bengo Atari, Tomoyo Matsumura, and Kenichi Tsujita. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum with detailed analyses of coronary artery disease. JACC Case Reports, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaccas.2023.101894, doi:10.1016/j.jaccas.2023.101894.

contexts.context: This excerpt is about validation of the PRAISE score for predicting adverse events after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) treated with PCI. It reports that higher predicted risk was associated with substantially higher all-cause mortality and recurrent myocardial infarction, and it also assessed major bleeding. Specifically, the high-risk group had increased risk of death (HR 12.24) and recurrent AMI (HR 3.92). The model’s discrimination for death, MI, and major bleeding was only modest (C-statistics 0.75, 0.61, 0.62), and the authors concluded its overall prognostic value was limited and that better models are needed.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?

Coronary artery calcifications on routine trauma CT were associated with a higher risk of in-hospital complications. Left main coronary artery calcification was independently associated with developing any complication, with an odds ratio of 3.9 (95% CI 1.7–8.9). An increasing number of calcified coronary arteries showed a graded trend toward more complications, indicating a burden–response relationship. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

The complications described included general clinical complications such as pneumonia and delirium. In addition, more extensive coronary calcification was significantly associated with an adverse discharge condition on the Glasgow Outcome Scale, suggesting worse short-term functional outcome at discharge. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

Overall, the available evidence indicates that coronary artery calcification is a marker of elevated peri-trauma risk, identifying patients more likely to develop clinical complications and to have poorer discharge outcomes. Pulmonary emphysema and aortic calcifications were not associated with complications in this cohort. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)
